title: Teacher Expertise Is Not Just Knowledge
author: Dr Haili Hughes
summary: Haili Hughes argues that CPD built mainly on transmitting information or strategies rests on too narrow a view of teacher expertise, which she recasts as trained interpretation and professional perception. She draws on embodied predictive processing to describe teaching as continuous anticipation and adjustment, with expert teachers holding richer mental models that let them read small cues. She extends this to the embodied side of teaching (positioning, gesture, pause, circulation) that cannot be developed by reading alone. She then uses social cognition to explain why pupils who have experienced adversity may read ordinary classroom events very differently, and why expert teachers hold several interpretations before acting. The combined move is a model of CPD as the development of professional perception, built through video analysis, rehearsal, coaching and case discussion. For school leaders, that means CPD that is sustained, close to practice, rehearsal-based and equipped with a shared language for interpreting learning and behaviour.
points: Hughes reframes teacher expertise as learned professional perception, such as noticing a pupil has stopped writing before disruption or hearing uncertainty in a confident answer, rather than mystical intuition.

The hard part of any strategy is not persuading teachers to use it but knowing when it is needed, how to adapt it and what evidence will show it is working, which calls for cycles of anticipation, action, evidence and adjustment.
Because teaching is embodied (where teachers stand, gesture, pause and circulate), CPD must include rehearsal of enacted routines, not just discussion of principles.

Social cognition explains why the same correction can be heard as support by one pupil and humiliation by another, so CPD should help teachers compare interpretations rather than issue generic calls to 'be trauma-informed.'
For leaders, she argues CPD should be sustained rather than episodic, close to classroom practice, rehearsal-based and grounded in a shared language for interpreting learning and behaviour.
quotes: Teacher expertise is not only a matter of knowing more. It also involves perceiving classroom situations differently.

They may see that a behaviour issue is partly about status, that a misconception has persisted beneath correct answers, or that a task has created unnecessary ambiguity. These judgements are not mystical forms of intuition; they are learned forms of professional perception.
Expertise, in this sense, involves better prediction and better updating. Expert teachers have built richer mental models of classrooms because they have encountered many similar patterns before.

This is one reason why coaching, video analysis, rehearsal, lesson study and structured reflection can be more powerful than one off presentations. They create opportunities for teachers to refine perception, not just collect techniques.
These practices cannot be fully developed by reading about them. They require rehearsal, feedback and refinement.

A correction may be heard as support by one pupil and humiliation by another. A raised voice may be experienced as firm direction by one pupil and threat by another. Group work may feel collaborative to some pupils and unsafe to others.

CPD can help develop this kind of judgement, but only if it moves beyond generic exhortations to “build relationships” or “be trauma-informed”. Teachers need concrete opportunities to analyse behaviour, compare interpretations, rehearse responses and understand the limits of their role. They are not therapists and should not be encouraged to diagnose pupils informally.
